source.citation: The Revised Municipal Code of Chicago of 1905. Passed March 20, 1905. Revised and codified by Edgar Bronson Tolman, Corporation Counsel, assisted by William H. Arthur and Roswell B. Mason. Chicago: published by authority of the City Council (book form October 15, 1905); Rochester, N.Y.: The Lawyers' Co-operative Publishing Company, 1905.
what_it_does_not_supply: The sidewalk actually laid on any particular block, or its date: every width in sec. 2072 yields to 'a different width ... specified in the order', and a block-level special-assessment ordinance or photograph is what would say what Prairie Avenue had
The width of a walk within the sidewalk space: the code lists permitted walk widths and chooses none
Any material for a particular block (T-1728 owns the surfaces)
The curb's reveal (its height above the gutter) or the roadway's crown
Whether the sections were in force in exactly this form on 1 July 1904; the code is dated 20 March 1905
what_it_supplies: The city's default width of the sidewalk space (street line to curb line) on a street of a given width: 14 ft on streets 66 to 80 ft wide, 10 ft on streets 50 to 60 ft wide (sec. 2072)
Where a walk stands inside that space: one foot from and parallel with the lot line, unless a special ordinance says otherwise (sec. 2062)
The walk widths the city's paving specification anticipates (5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 18, 20, 24 and 25 ft; sec. 2062), which bound a reconstructed walk width
That the rest of the sidewalk space could be a planted court or grass plat (sec. 2077), i.e. a parkway
The curb's minimum thickness where one was required (3 in, stone or white oak; sec. 2072) and the cross-fall of the sidewalk space (1 in in 3 ft toward the curb; the 'Slope' sections, pp. 552-553)
